Vanguard Intermediate-Term Corporate Bond ETF (NASDAQ:VCIT) offers a higher yield and lower expense ratio than iShares National Muni Bond ETF (NYSEMKT:MUB), but it introduces corporate credit risk and historically higher volatility.

Fixed-income investors often choose between the tax advantages of municipal bonds and the higher yields available in the corporate debt market. While both funds provide relative stability compared to equities, their tax treatments and risk profiles differ significantly due to the nature of their underlying issuers.

What's inside

Vanguard Intermediate-Term Corporate Bond ETF invests in U.S. dollar-denominated investment-grade fixed income securities issued by industrial, utility, and financial companies. The fund contains 2,342 holdings with maturities between five and 10 years and tracks its index using a representative sampling technique. No single position in the portfolio exceeds 0.29% of assets. It was launched in 2009. The Vanguard fund has paid $4.34 per share over the trailing 12 months, which on its recent ~$79.24 share price works out to a 5.5% yield.

iShares National Muni Bond ETF focuses on high-quality municipal bonds issued across the United States by state and local governments. Its massive portfolio includes 7,938 holdings, ranging from money market instruments to long-term revenue bonds for universities and water utilities. It was launched in 2007. The iShares fund has paid $3.70 per share over the trailing 12 months, which on its recent ~$103.90 share price works out to a 3.6% yield.

title: How Big Could Cloudflare Stock's Next Fall Be?
detail:
How Big Could Cloudflare Stock's Next Fall Be?
Trefis Team

ZS

Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Cloudflare (NET) stock lost 12.8% in the month to November 10, 2026, against 3.6% for the S&P 500, in a month when Akamai Technologies, Zscaler and Palo Alto Networks also fell. Buyers still pay 40 times the company's sales over the past year, betting that its growth keeps accelerating and its reported losses turn into profits. When markets sold off before, how much did Cloudflare stock give up, and for how long?

How Deep Did Cloudflare Stock Fall In Past Sell-Offs?

The 2022 inflation shock hit Cloudflare stock hardest: it fell 69%, while the S&P 500 fell 24%. Its largest fall at any time since its listing was deeper still: 82.6%, from its close on November 18, 2021, to its close on November 9, 2022. The market figures in this section are measured on the SPY fund, which tracks the index. Across the six market shocks the stock has traded through since its 2019 listing, it lost 30.7% on average, against 16.8% for the index. It fell further than the S&P 500 in all but one of them, the 2020 COVID-19 crash. The most recent, the 2025 tariff shock, took 40% off the stock against 19% off the index.

Cloudflare stock eventually returned to its pre-decline high every time. The median climb back from the low took 1.2 months, but recovering from the 2022 fall took 31.4 months, from its June 2022 low until January 2025. The stock closed lower still in November 2022 before that climb.

Cloudflare's Sales Are Growing Faster Than A Year Ago

Revenue rose 39.2% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026, against 30.7% growth in the same quarter of 2025, so the faster growth buyers are counting on has held so far. Management said the quarter's growth came in particular from its Workers Developer Platform, from AI agent workloads across its network and from its largest customers. Customers that management counts as large brought in 75% of revenue, up from 73% a year earlier.

Cloudflare Still Reports Losses, And Gross Margin Is Slipping

Based on the figures in its filings, Cloudflare still lost money in fiscal Q3 2026. Its operating loss was 7.3% of revenue, slightly wider than the 6.7% of revenue reported a year earlier. On management's adjusted measure, the operating margin reached 17.5%, the highest in the company's history.

Management expects Cloudflare to turn a GAAP profit in fiscal Q4 2026, arriving earlier than the 2028 deadline it set at its 2026 Investor Day. That profit remains a forecast.

Gross margin is lower than a year ago. Management said the adjusted measure fell to 72.4% in fiscal Q3 2026, down 290 basis points from a year earlier. That level remains inside the company's long-term target range of 70% to 77%. Management also said its Workers product has slightly lower gross margins than products such as Zero Trust, though it costs much less to sell.

IREN (NASDAQ:IREN), a vertically integrated data center operator, closed at $20.84, up 5.63%. The stock rose as AI cloud peers gained, with CoreWeave's strong results easing financing and demand concerns. Investors are watching IREN's AI cloud execution and its next update on Microsoft deliveries and spending plans.
Trading volume reached 80.3M shares, coming in about 58% above its three-month average of 50.7M shares. IREN IPO'd in 2021 and has fallen 15% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 closed at 7,618, up 1.29%, while the Nasdaq Composite closed at 25,466, up 1.60%. Among AI cloud infrastructure and Bitcoin mining data centers, Core Scientific closed at $14.57, up 10.97%, and Cipher Digital closed at $7.11, up 8.88%, showing the same sector rotation that lifted IREN.

What this means for investors

As previously stated, IREN's rise was likely in response to CoreWeave, which delivered a stellar earnings report that showed growth, pricing power, and, most importantly, the ability to manage financing.

Financing has become critical to neocloud-oriented cloud stocks, which have run massive losses as they ramp up spending to meet the insatiable demand for AI-specific cloud infrastructure.

Moreover, the stock rose even though CoreWeave's success did not directly address IREN's struggles. This is critical, since, in recent weeks, investors soured on IREN stock amid a $4 billion ARR target that had slipped.

Also, news that some infrastructure deliveries to Microsoft were delayed due to requested modifications. Although that was likely not IREN's fault, it served as a reminder that delays could negatively affect IREN due to its heavy reliance on credit.

Indeed, investors can breathe a sigh of relief, as the rally takes some near-term pressure off IREN and its peers. Nonetheless, a funding gap remains, and amid rapid growth, the stock is unlikely to be out of the woods as it seeks to capitalize on that growth while meeting its considerable debt obligations.

Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX), an orbital launch and satellite broadband services provider better known as SpaceX, closed at $139.75, down 2.33%. Reports that the FCC accepted SpaceX's nationwide spectrum application and a separate Singulus equipment order supported premarket trading, while investors are watching Friday's Starship Flight 15.

Trading volume reached 111.2 million shares, coming in nearly 15% above its three-month average of 96.9 million shares. SpaceX IPO'd in 2026 and has fallen 13% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) closed at 7,619, up 1.31%, and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) closed at 25,466, up 1.60%. What this means for investors

On Wednesday, Nov. 11, SpaceX shares ended below premarket highs that were driven by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission formally accepting the company's application to acquire 800 MHz spectrum licenses from Grain Management on Nov. 10. This is a key milestone since it clears the first regulatory hurdle for the company to transition from a satellite partner to telecom conglomerates into a stand-alone, nationwide wireless carrier.

However, these early gains faded as investors shifted focus on SpaceX's upcoming Starship test flight scheduled for Friday, Nov. 13. The massive, reusable Starship rocket is critical for deploying next-gen Starlink satellites, and eventually, launching orbital data centers to power the artificial intelligence boom. Consequently, the high-stakes launch introduces near-term execution and technical risk that pushed SpaceX shares down.

Another factor weighing on the stock is the impending insider lockup period set to expire on Dec. 8. After this date, the market could be flooded with additional tradable shares.

SpaceX delivered spectacular performance in its third-quarter earnings report, announced Oct. 20. The company achieved 161% year-over-year revenue growth to $14.6 billion, with $7.6 billion of that generated by its AI business.

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), the leading manufacturer of artificial intelligence (AI) chips and data center computing systems, rebounded 2.87% on Wednesday, November 11, closing at $173.73 as strong earnings from CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) helped restore confidence in the AI trade. The rally followed Tuesday's steep sell-off, with investors finding renewed optimism in CoreWeave's surging revenue and growing demand for AI infrastructure.

Trading volume reached 266.6 million shares, more than double its three-month daily average of 129.6 million, underscoring strong investor interest in the rebound. With Nvidia scheduled to report earnings on November 17, attention is turning to whether the chipmaker can sustain its growth momentum amid ongoing concerns about China restrictions and uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang.

How the markets moved today

Wall Street rebounded sharply on Wednesday, with technology stocks leading the recovery following Tuesday's inflation-driven sell-off. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) climbed 1.29% to 7,618, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) advanced 1.60% to 25,466.

Semiconductor stocks were among the session's strongest performers, with Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) surging 7.32% to $552.90 and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) gaining 3.99% to $345.22. Both outperformed Nvidia, suggesting the rally extended beyond a single company as investors regained confidence in the broader AI industry.

What this means for investors

Wednesday's rebound suggests investors remain confident in the long-term outlook for AI infrastructure, despite recent volatility. CoreWeave's stronger-than-expected results and improved revenue guidance provide encouraging evidence that demand for computing capacity continues to outpace available supply. As a major supplier of the GPUs powering these data centers, Nvidia stands to benefit from sustained infrastructure investment.

However, the rally doesn't eliminate the risks facing Nvidia. Baird downgraded the stock to Neutral on Wednesday, citing uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang, potential restrictions on chip exports to China, and slowing growth in hyperscaler capital expenditures heading into 2027. These concerns could weigh on Nvidia's valuation even if near-term demand remains strong.

Nvidia's November 17 earnings report will provide a critical test of its growth outlook. Investors should focus on data center revenue, profit margins, and management's forward guidance, particularly whether demand for next-generation chips remains strong enough to offset potential weakness in China. Strong results could help sustain the recovery, but longer-term confidence will also depend on greater clarity surrounding Huang's leadership and the regulatory outlook.

title: History Says 1 Month Has Been the S&P 500's Most Reliable Since 1950. It's Only Weeks Away.
detail:
History Says 1 Month Has Been the S&P 500's Most Reliable Since 1950. It's Only Weeks Away.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool

The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT:VOO) has had a bumpy November. The fund slid more than 4% on Thursday, Nov. 5, in a sell-off led by chipmakers and other tech shares. It then gained over 2% on Monday, Nov. 9.

Investors worried the midterm election results might slow the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI). As of this writing, the fund trades near $692, down about 4% from the 52-week high it set at $718.47.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

A rocky patch going into the holidays can have investors checking the calendar for some reassurance. And here, the history is encouraging.

Since 1950, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) has ended December up in 55 of 76 years. That's a 72% hit rate, and no other month has a better one.

I counted every month from 1950 through 2025 with the index's month-end closes from Yahoo Finance, on price only, without dividends. December came first, but not by much. And its record in the past decade looks far more ordinary.

Image source: Getty Images.

December edges out November and April

Two other months are close. April and November each ended higher in 53 of 76 years, or around 70%. Over all 912 months in the record, the index climbed about 61% of the time.

September was the worst month by far. It gained in just 34 of 76 years and averaged a drop of around 0.6%, making it one of only two months (along with February) with an average decline.

Put another way, December has had around nine more up years than a typical month would have across the same stretch.

Notably, December doesn't hold the highest average gain. That goes to November, at around 1.9%. December averaged a rise of around 1.4%, which is still almost double the 0.7% or so in a typical month.

How bad can December get?

The down Decembers have been rarer, but they haven't all been mild. The index dropped around 9.2% in December 2018 -- the worst December of the 76 years I checked. It also lost about 6% in December 2002 and about 5.9% in December 2022. But 10 of the 21 losing Decembers cost the index under 2%.

Each of the three worst had something bigger going on. The year 2002 was the third straight losing year of the dot-com crash, and the index finished it down around 23%. And in both 2018 and 2022, the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates in the middle of December, on Dec. 19 and Dec. 14, respectively.
